title: Drug Interactions: CYP Inhibitors vs Inducers

questions.stem: A patient stable on warfarin starts rifampin. What dose change will likely be needed?
questions.explanation: A is correct: rifampin is an inducer, so warfarin levels fall and the clotting test drops; monitor closely and raise the dose. B is what an inhibitor would need. C misses a strong interaction. D removes needed protection from clots.

questions.stem: The same patient later stops rifampin. What happens to the warfarin dose?
questions.explanation: A is correct: when rifampin stops, lower the warfarin dose again, because the extra enzyme wears off and warfarin levels rise. B would push levels even higher and raise bleeding risk. C ignores the loss of induction. D changes timing but not the amount.

questions.stem: Which of these can push up the level of another drug cleared by liver enzymes? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: B, C, E, and F are correct: clarithromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, and grapefruit juice inhibit the enzyme, so other drugs pile up. A, rifampin, and D, Saint John's wort, are inducers that push levels down.

questions.stem: Which are classic strong inducers? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: B, C, D, and E are correct: rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and Saint John's wort are strong inducers. A, clarithromycin, is a strong inhibitor.

questions.stem: A patient on simvastatin is prescribed clarithromycin. What is the main risk?
questions.explanation: D is correct: clarithromycin is a strong inhibitor, so simvastatin piles up and raises the risk of muscle breakdown. A, statin failure, is the risk with an inducer, not an inhibitor. B and C are not effects of a raised simvastatin level.

questions.stem: Rifampin is started today in a patient on a drug cleared by liver enzymes. When is the full drop in that drug's level expected?

options.text: Never; inducers act only on the first dose

questions.explanation: B is correct: induction is slow, often about 1 to 2 weeks to build up and to wear off. A and C describe a much faster change; even inhibitors take days. D is wrong because induction builds over time and lasts while the inducer is taken.

questions.stem: A patient taking a combined birth control pill starts rifampin. What is the main concern?
questions.explanation: A is correct: an inducer pushes the other drug down, with a risk of drug failure, like a failed birth control pill. B is the risk with an inhibitor. C is not the effect taught for this pair. D misses a known interaction.

questions.stem: A patient takes ciprofloxacin and an antacid at the same time each morning. What is the best advice?

options.text: Separate the doses by several hours

questions.explanation: D is correct: calcium, magnesium, iron, and antacids bind fluoroquinolones in the gut, so separate the doses by several hours. A adds calcium, which also binds ciprofloxacin. C raises the dose instead of fixing the binding. B lets the binding continue.

questions.stem: A patient takes levothyroxine and an iron tablet together every morning. Why is this a problem?

options.text: Iron binds levothyroxine, so less is absorbed

questions.explanation: A is correct: iron binds levothyroxine in the gut, so less gets absorbed. B and C describe enzyme effects, but this interaction is binding, not enzymes. D misses the interaction.

questions.stem: A strong enzyme inhibitor is added to a patient's regimen. What is the main risk for the other drug?

options.text: Level falls and the drug fails
Level rises and toxicity risk goes up
The drug binds in the gut

questions.explanation: B is correct: an inhibitor pushes the other drug level up, fast, with toxicity risk. A describes an inducer. C describes the slow timing of induction, while inhibitors act within days. D describes binding with cations, a different interaction.
